answer_text:
Let

\[
T(u)=\int_0^u \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx.
\]

For \(u\ge 0\),

\[
T(u)=\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_0^u=2\sqrt{u}.
\]

If the infinite nested integral has value \(I\), then the expression inside the upper limit of the outermost integral is the same infinite nested integral. Hence the value must satisfy the self-similarity equation

\[
I=T(I)=2\sqrt{I}.
\]

Since \(I\ge 0\), let \(y=\sqrt{I}\). Then

\[
y^2=2y,
\]

so

\[
y(y-2)=0.
\]

Thus

\[
y=0 \quad\text{or}\quad y=2,
\]

which gives

\[
I=0 \quad\text{or}\quad I=4.
\]

The value \(I=0\) is the degenerate fixed point obtained by terminating the nesting at \(0\). For the nondegenerate infinite nesting, consider finite truncations with any positive innermost upper limit \(a>0\). If

\[
I_0=a,\qquad I_{n+1}=2\sqrt{I_n},
\]

then

\[
I_n=4\left(\frac{a}{4}\right)^{1/2^n}\to 4
\]

as \(n\to\infty\). Therefore the infinite nested integral evaluates to

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
